question: The order of the amino acids in a chain, written from the amino end to the carboxyl end, is a protein's _____, and the gene's nucleotide order fixes it.
questions: Swapping one glutamate for a valine at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain is a change to _____ that produces haemoglobin S and, inherited twice, sickle cell anaemia.
Deep mutational scanning measures thousands of variants of one protein at once, which is a way of asking which changes to _____ actually matter.
abstract:
The primary structure of a protein is the order of the amino acids along its chain, and that order is the defining characteristic of a protein: not a class of similar molecules but one particular sequence. It is written from the amino terminus to the carboxyl terminus, which is the order the chain is built in. Nor is it the protein's own choice, since the sequence is determined by the order of nucleotides in the gene that encodes it. A single position in that order can matter enormously, and in the sickle cell mutation a negatively charged glutamate is replaced by a neutral valine at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain, a substitution Vernon Ingram identified in 1956 by a fingerprinting technique. The result is haemoglobin S, and inheriting the variant from both parents gives sickle cell anaemia, the commonest and most severe form of the disease.

It does not follow that every substitution behaves that way, and the globin genes, HBB above all, carry a wide spread of variants whose relations to the clinical picture are complicated enough to make diagnosis genuinely difficult. Which changes matter is now measured rather than argued about, since deep mutational scanning assays many thousands of variants of a single protein in one pooled experiment. Those results are used to classify clinical variants and to test how well the predictive models actually do. Reading a sequence has changed as much, and single-molecule instruments now probe individual peptides in real time, at single amino acid resolution, rather than working on bulk samples. They do not replace mass spectrometry, because neither approach on its own achieves full coverage of a sequence.
